metadata.title: Oracle Has a Debt Fever & the Only Prescription is More Debt

content.text:
Our analysts just identified a stock with the potential to be the next Nvidia. Tell us how you invest and we'll show you why it's our #1 pick. Tap here.
Oracle on Thursday told investors it needs another $20 billion for AI infrastructure on top of the $20 billion it said it needed earlier this year. Oh, and they reported $23.7 billion of negative free cash flow for the year.
Investors are growing weary of the debt and equity dilution companies like Oracle keep taking on to finance AI-infra that, so far, burns money instead of making it. Worse, the builders have lost faith in their own balance sheets, which have always been their true religion, tapping debt and equity markets because they don't have the cash to keep the bubble inflated.
WHAT HAPPENED
Oracle's latest earnings weren't all bad, but given its record-breaking level of obligations and shaky cash flow, we can see why the market reacted the way it did. Especially when they said they wanted to pile on even more.
The company beat on the top and bottom lines, with revenue coming in at $19.18 billion, a 21% jump, topping average analyst estimates. Oracle also hit its adjusted EPS of $ 2.03, above the $1.96 average estimate, but that's because it left out all the bad stuff. Oracle's GAAP EPS came in at $1.45, short of the expected range, with a $0.66-per-share gap due to stock-based compensation, past acquisitions, taxes, and, of course, restructuring and other costs, which totaled $0.30, $0.15 less than stock compensation.
Their operating cash flow for FY 2026 was strong too, coming in at $32 billion, up 54%. But don't get too excited: Investors had to watch the entire haul disappear into the data center buildout, and drag-free cash flow to negative $23.7 billion. The business is technically making money, but the buildout is spending it faster than it comes in. Oracle looks caught in the worst kind of sunk-cost fallacy, forcing them to point to a horizon-filled AI while they try to pile on more cash, saying, "Trust me, bro."
WHY IT MATTERS
If we add up Oracle's entire stack of obligations, we're looking at roughly $130 billion in borrowing, plus another $135 billion or so in data center leases they have already signed for, locked in for 15 years. This puts Oracle's total obligations somewhere near a quarter of a trillion dollars, with only $32 billion in operating cash flow instantly negated when they announced cash flow was, in fact, negative.
One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.
Oracle hopefuls will say, "Well, what about their remaining performance obligations (RPO)? That's $638 billion, far outweighing what they owe." That figure was on the first line of their investor report, a subtle way of saying look at this and nothing else. That said, they have to build to actually collect that $638 billion. And given news broke Thursday from Bloomberg that Crusoe, one of Oracle's biggest landlords and data center builders, just got "pushed aside" after trying to construct an AI campus in Wyoming, it doesn't bode well for confidence. If execution delays hit the broader supply chain, Oracle faces even more financial exposure.
Since we're on the topic of financial exposure, we should talk about OpenAI. Media reports from this week indicate they're preparing to cut costs by lowering the fees it charges businesses for API access and tokens in an effort to compete with Anthropic. This will result in an even higher cash burn rate for the company, destroying any chance for OpenAI to actually turn a profit due to high inference costs. Amazon did the same thing in early 2014 and sure, it worked out, but can the same strategy work twice? Probably not. The Information reports that OpenAI's adjusted negative margins sit at approximately -122%. Which means for every dollar of revenue OpenAI generated, it lost an additional $1.22, which is bad for Oracle because OpenAI accounts for a reported $300 billion of Oracle's RPOs, or almost half. If OpenAI can't pay up in mid-2027 per the newly released financial disclosures, what happens then?
WHAT'S NEXT
One would assume more capital raises, and if OpenAI can get there, a move into the public markets. But the payments that would justify Oracle's spending only arrive gradually.
Look at how they're funding it. In fiscal 2026, Oracle leaned hard on the bond market, roughly $43 billion in new debt. Now, for fiscal 2027, it's flipping the mix toward equity, that $20 billion at-the-market program, with another debt tranche queued up for 2027. In other words, they're scrambling to find cash literally anywhere to keep this pain-train going.
Raising more may look like the easy lever, but even SoftBank's Masayoshi Son couldn't pull it. His push to borrow $6 billion against SoftBank's OpenAI stake stalled when lenders balked at valuing a private company as collateral, and that was after he'd already trimmed the ask from $10 billion.
Hedge funds, private credit, and the rest of the money are turning from bullish to cautious, because they smell something rotten in the circular financing all of these companies believed made them unstoppable.
